lines.text: The final notice said payment was overdue and service would stop unless money arrived by a date. That was the whole warning.
It did not tell the recipient that a billing dispute might be discussed with company representatives before the service stopped.
The omission mattered because a phone line, employees, credit counselors, and payment arrangements existed elsewhere in the system.
But lower courts found that the relevant procedure had not been adequately explained or made available to Mary Craft when she sought help.
The Supreme Court said a sufficient cutoff notice should state where, during which hours, and before whom a disputed bill could be considered.
That holding changed the information supplied before termination. It did not decide whether the Crafts owed the disputed amount.
It also did not eliminate termination: after notice and an opportunity to be heard, the utility could still cut service if the bill was justly due.
The defect was therefore visible on the page itself: a deadline and a threat, with the path to a human decision-maker left blank.
